variants.name: Callables with all()/any()
variants.implementation_notes: Python rules are callables: a leaf is a function or lambda (a partial or bound method for parameterized rules), composition is `all(rule(c) for rule in rules)` or `any(...)`, and the built-ins filter() plus comprehensions consume them directly. A named def gives the rule its domain name (def is_overdue(invoice, days=30)), a factory closes over the parameters, and functools.partial/operator helpers cover the reusable plumbing. The class form - a Specification with is_satisfied_by and __and__/__or__/__invert__ - is still reasonable when rules must be introspected, hashed, pickled, or translated into a query (SQLAlchemy's and_/or_/not_ combinators play the same role for the database side); otherwise it is ceremony around a callable.
pitfalls: A list comprehension over rules evaluates every rule; all()/any() over a generator short-circuits, so pick the form deliberately for expensive rules.
Lambdas are opaque: no name, no introspection and no explanation of why a candidate failed; a named function or class is needed when the rule must explain itself.
Rules may raise instead of returning False (AttributeError on a None candidate), which is not a predicate; guard the candidate type or wrap the boundary.
Mutable default arguments and closures over reassigned variables make a rule stateful between calls.

variants.name: Specification classes with operator overloads
variants.implementation_notes: The classic object form carried into Python: an immutable class (typically a frozen dataclass) per rule exposing is_satisfied_by(candidate), combinators returning new _And/_Or/_Not instances, and operator overloads so that `rule_a & ~rule_b` reads like the rule. Python's dataclasses/attrs make the parameters explicit and give equality and repr for logging, hashing is available for rule deduplication, and the class is introspectable where a lambda is not. Choose it over bare callables when rules are named domain concepts that must be described, cached, pickled or translated; local one-off checks stay callables.
pitfalls: __and__/__or__ must return new instances; mutating and returning self leaks state into every composite that shares the instance.
Operator precedence surprises: & binds tighter than |, so mixed expressions need parentheses and are easy to misread.
Work in __init__ (I/O, loading configuration, reading the clock) turns rule construction into a hidden side effect and breaks the value-object assumption.
Dataclass equality is structural: two rules with equal parameters compare equal, which is useful for caching but surprising if identity was expected.
